q: The graph shows the pressure variation at one point as a sound wave passes. If the wavelength of this sound is 1.36 m, what is its speed?
e: One full cycle takes 4.0 ms on the graph, so T = 4.0 × 10⁻³ s and f = 1/T = 250 Hz.
t: On a time graph, crest-to-crest is the PERIOD, not the wavelength.

q: A Lineweaver–Burk plot crosses the x-axis at −0.50 mM⁻¹. What is Km?
e: x-intercept = −1/Km
−1/Km = −0.50 mM⁻¹, so Km = 2.0 mM

q: At 37 °C (where 2.303RT ≈ 5.9 kJ mol⁻¹), an enzyme lowers a reaction's activation energy by about 18 kJ mol⁻¹. Assuming the Arrhenius pre-factor is unchanged, by roughly what factor does the rate increase?
e: k ∝ 10<sup>−E<sub>a</sub>/(2.303RT)</sup>, so the rate ratio is 10<sup>ΔE<sub>a</sub>/(2.303RT)</sup>.
18/5.9 ≈ 3, so the rate increases by about 10³ = 1000-fold.
t: Each ~6 kJ mol⁻¹ off E<sub>a</sub> at body temperature ≈ 10× faster.

q: An enzyme has V<sub>max</sub> = 50 µM s⁻¹. What is the initial rate when [S] = K<sub>m</sub>/4?
e: v = V<sub>max</sub>[S]/(K<sub>m</sub> + [S]) = 50 × (0.25K<sub>m</sub>)/(1.25K<sub>m</sub>).

q: An enzyme follows Michaelis–Menten kinetics. At [S] = 3Km, what fraction of Vmax is the reaction rate?
e: v = Vmax[S] ÷ (Km + [S])
= Vmax(3Km) ÷ (Km + 3Km) = 3/4 Vmax

q: What does an enzyme’s Km represent in Michaelis–Menten kinetics?
e: At [S] = Km, v = Vmax/2 for Michaelis–Menten behavior.

q: Alcohol dehydrogenase converts ethanol and NAD⁺ into acetaldehyde and NADH. To which enzyme class does it belong?
e: Ethanol is oxidized while NAD⁺ is reduced.
Enzymes that catalyze redox reactions (dehydrogenases, oxidases, reductases) are oxidoreductases.

q: Trypsinogen is cleaved by enteropeptidase to form active trypsin. Trypsinogen is an example of a:
e: Zymogens are inactive precursors activated by cleavage.
Making digestive proteases as zymogens keeps them from digesting the pancreas.

q: An enzyme has V<sub>max</sub> = 60 µM s⁻¹ and gives v = 40 µM s⁻¹ at [S] = 2.0 mM. What is K<sub>m</sub>?
With substrate in large excess and all other conditions constant, the total enzyme concentration is doubled. What happens?
o: V<sub>max</sub> is unchanged; K<sub>m</sub> is halved
e: V<sub>max</sub> = k<sub>cat</sub>[E]<sub>T</sub>, so doubling [E]<sub>T</sub> doubles V<sub>max</sub>.
K<sub>m</sub> is a property of each enzyme molecule and its substrate, so it stays the same.

q: An allosteric enzyme with cooperative substrate binding shows what kind of rate vs. [S] curve?
e: Binding at one site makes binding at other sites easier.
This gives a sigmoidal curve, like hemoglobin's O₂-binding curve.

q: A mixed inhibitor binds the enzyme–substrate complex much more tightly than it binds free enzyme. How do apparent K<sub>m</sub> and V<sub>max</sub> change?
o: K<sub>m</sub> increases and V<sub>max</sub> is unchanged
K<sub>m</sub> is unchanged and V<sub>max</sub> increases
e: Any inhibitor that binds ES lowers V<sub>max</sub>.
Preferring ES pulls E + S → ES forward, so the enzyme appears to bind S more tightly: apparent K<sub>m</sub> falls (like uncompetitive inhibition).

q: Enzyme 1: kcat = 100 s⁻¹, Km = 1.0 mM. Enzyme 2: kcat = 1000 s⁻¹, Km = 100 mM. Which is the more efficient catalyst at low [S]?
e: Catalytic efficiency = kcat/Km.
Enzyme 1 is 10× more efficient.

q: In collagen, every third residue is glycine. Replacing one of these glycines (as in some forms of brittle bone disease) weakens the triple helix. Why?
o: Only glycine's tiny side chain fits in the crowded helix center
Glycine forms the disulfides that link the three chains
Glycine is the residue that vitamin C–dependent enzymes hydroxylate
Glycine's charged side chain repels water from the helix
e: In the triple helix, every third residue faces the packed center where the three chains meet.
Only glycine (side chain = H) fits there; any larger side chain pushes the strands apart.

q: Amino acids in human proteins have which configuration at the α-carbon?
o: A racemic mix of D and L
e: Proteins in humans are built almost entirely from L-amino acids.
Most are (S) by the Cahn–Ingold–Prelog system; cysteine is the (R) exception.

q: A cysteine thiol in a peptide has pK<sub>a</sub> = 8.3. At pH 7.3, what is the approximate ratio of thiolate (–S⁻) to thiol (–SH)?
e: [–S⁻]/[–SH] = 10⁻¹, so the ratio is 1 : 10; most cysteines are still –SH.
t: pH below pK<sub>a</sub> → protonated form wins; each pH unit = factor of 10.

q: Cysteine and methionine both contain sulfur. How do their side chains differ?
o: Cys has a thiol (–SH); Met has a thioether (–S–CH₃)
Met has a thiol (–SH); Cys has a thioether (–S–)
Both are thiols, but only methionine can form disulfides
Both are thioethers, but only cysteine is aromatic
e: Cysteine: –CH₂–SH, which can oxidize to form disulfide bonds.
Methionine: –CH₂CH₂–S–CH₃, a nonpolar thioether that cannot form disulfides.

q: At a pH well below its isoelectric point, an amino acid generally has what net charge?
e: Acidic solution favors protonation, increasing positive charge.

q: At physiological pH, a free alanine molecule exists mainly as:
e: The carboxyl group (pKa ≈ 2) is deprotonated at pH 7.4.
The amino group (pKa ≈ 9–10) is still protonated.
So alanine carries both charges and is net neutral: a zwitterion.

q: A disulfide bond forms between two:
e: Two –SH groups are oxidized to form –S–S– (cystine).
Reducing agents like β-mercaptoethanol break disulfides.

q: Quaternary structure describes:
o: How multiple polypeptide subunits fit together
The folding of one chain into a 3D shape
e: Only proteins with more than one subunit (for example, hemoglobin's four chains) have quaternary structure.

q: Which standard amino acid is achiral?
e: A chiral α-carbon needs four different groups.
Glycine's side chain is just H, so its α-carbon has two identical H atoms.

q: Which two standard amino acids have side chains that end in an amide group (–CONH₂)?
e: Asparagine (Asn) and glutamine (Gln) carry –CONH₂ on their side chains.
Aspartate and glutamate have –COO⁻ instead; they are the acidic 'parents' of Asn and Gln.
t: Asn/Gln = 'amide twins' of Asp/Glu: swap –O⁻ for –NH₂.

q: Lysine has pKa values of 2.2 (α-COOH), 9.0 (α-NH₃⁺) and 10.5 (side-chain NH₃⁺). What is its pI?
e: For a basic amino acid, average the two amino-group pKa values.

q: In a β-pleated sheet, where do the side chains of consecutive residues along one strand point?
o: Alternately above and below the plane of the sheet
All toward the neighboring strand to form H-bonds
All outward from a central axis, as in a helix
All into the sheet's plane, between the strands
e: The backbone N–H and C=O groups make the H-bonds between strands, within the plane.
Side chains alternate up and down, so one face of a sheet can be nonpolar and the other polar.
t: Helix: side chains point out like bristles; sheet: they alternate up and down.

q: A reactive oxygen species converts one guanine into 8-oxoguanine without distorting the helix. Which repair pathway most directly removes this damaged base?
e: Base excision repair starts with a DNA glycosylase that removes a single damaged base; the gap is then filled and sealed.
Nucleotide excision repair handles bulky, helix-distorting lesions such as thymine dimers; mismatch repair fixes replication errors; NHEJ joins double-strand breaks.
t: One bad base → BER. Bulky bump in the helix → NER. Wrong partner after copying → MMR.

q: A cloning plasmid carries a gene for ampicillin resistance. After a transformation, the bacteria are spread on plates containing ampicillin. Why?
o: Only cells that took up the plasmid can grow
Ampicillin makes the bacteria take up more plasmid
Ampicillin cuts the plasmid so the insert can enter
Only cells without the plasmid can grow
e: Transformation is inefficient; most cells take up no plasmid.
The resistance gene lets plasmid-carrying cells survive on ampicillin, so every colony that grows contains the plasmid.

q: A researcher wants to compare how much mRNA for one particular gene is made in liver versus muscle. Which technique fits best?
e: A Northern blot uses a labeled probe to detect a specific RNA after gel separation (RT-qPCR is a modern alternative).
Southern blots detect DNA, Western blots detect proteins, and sequencing reads a DNA sequence.
t: SNoW DRoP: Southern–DNA, Northern–RNA, Western–Protein.

q: Histones bind DNA tightly mainly because they:
o: Are rich in positive lysine and arginine, which attract DNA's negative backbone
Are rich in negative aspartate and glutamate, which bind DNA's nitrogenous bases
Form covalent bonds between their lysine side chains and DNA's bases
Are rich in hydrophobic residues that insert between DNA's stacked bases
e: DNA's phosphate backbone is negatively charged.
Positive histone tails attract it; acetylating those lysines loosens the grip and promotes transcription.

q: A drug inhibits histone deacetylases (HDACs) in cultured cells. What is the most likely effect?
o: Chromatin opens up and transcription of many genes increases
Chromatin condenses and transcription of many genes stops
Histones gain extra positive charge and bind DNA more tightly
The DNA sequence of affected genes is permanently mutated
e: Acetyl groups added to lysines remove their positive charge, loosening histone–DNA contact.
Blocking deacetylases keeps histones acetylated, so chromatin stays open (euchromatin) and transcription rises.

q: Why do linear chromosomes lose a little DNA from their ends with each round of replication if telomerase is absent?
o: The last RNA primer on the lagging strand can't be replaced with DNA
Leading-strand synthesis cannot begin at the chromosome's origin
Helicase cannot unwind the final few thousand base pairs
Ligase removes the terminal nucleotides after each round
e: After the RNA primer at the very end of the lagging strand is removed, there is no upstream 3′-OH for polymerase to extend into the gap.
That end stays short, so each round trims the chromosome (the end-replication problem).

q: The two strands of a DNA double helix are:
o: Joined by covalent bonds between bases
e: The strands run in opposite directions.
That's why replication needs a leading and a lagging strand.

q: Why is the lagging strand made as short, separate Okazaki fragments?
o: Polymerase works only 5′→3′, which runs away from the fork on that strand
Polymerase works only 3′→5′, which runs away from the fork on that strand
The lagging strand template is RNA, which must be copied in short pieces
Helicase unwinds the lagging strand only after the leading strand is done
e: The two template strands are antiparallel, but every new strand must grow 5′→3′.
On one strand that direction follows the fork (leading, continuous); on the other it points away, so synthesis restarts repeatedly as the fork opens (lagging, discontinuous).

q: When a DNA solution is slowly heated, its absorbance at 260 nm rises sharply near the melting temperature. Why?
o: Separated strands have unstacked bases, which absorb more UV light
Heat breaks the phosphodiester backbone into free nucleotides
Heat converts thymine into uracil, which absorbs more strongly
The DNA strands aggregate and scatter more light
e: Stacked bases in double-stranded DNA absorb less UV than unstacked ones.
When the strands separate, absorbance at 260 nm rises (the hyperchromic effect), so A₂₆₀ can track melting.

q: Bacteria grown in heavy ¹⁵N medium are moved to normal ¹⁴N medium and allowed to replicate once. What does their DNA look like in a density gradient?
o: All of it is hybrid (intermediate) density
Half of it is heavy and half of it is light
Half of it is hybrid and half of it is light
All of it is heavy, like the parent DNA
e: Semiconservative replication: each new helix keeps one old (¹⁵N) strand and gets one new (¹⁴N) strand.
After one round, every molecule is ¹⁵N/¹⁴N hybrid.

q: In agarose gel electrophoresis of DNA, which fragments travel farthest?
e: All DNA is negatively charged and moves toward the + electrode.
Smaller fragments slip through the gel's pores faster.

q: Which DNA molecule would have the highest melting temperature (Tm)?
e: G–C pairs have 3 hydrogen bonds and stack more strongly.
More G–C content means more energy is needed to separate the strands.

q: Introns are removed from pre-mRNA by the:
e: The spliceosome, made of snRNAs and proteins, cuts out introns and joins exons.

q: In E. coli, the sigma (σ) factor's main job is to:
o: Help RNA polymerase recognize and bind promoters
Unwind DNA ahead of the replication fork
Stop transcription at the end of a gene
Add the 5′ cap to new mRNA
e: The σ subunit joins the core RNA polymerase to form the holoenzyme, which recognizes −10 and −35 promoter sequences.
Once transcription begins, σ is usually released. Bacterial mRNA is not capped.

q: In bacteria, ribosomes can begin translating an mRNA before its transcription is finished, but this does not happen in human cells. Why?
o: Human transcription occurs in the nucleus, and translation in the cytoplasm
Human ribosomes can bind only the 3′ end of an mRNA
Bacterial mRNAs are made 3′→5′, so the start codon leaves the polymerase last
Human mRNAs have no start codon until they are spliced
e: Bacteria have no nucleus, so a new mRNA's 5′ end is exposed to ribosomes while RNA polymerase is still working.
In eukaryotes, pre-mRNA is capped, spliced and exported from the nucleus before ribosomes can reach it.

q: An E. coli strain has a lacI mutation that makes a nonfunctional repressor. When grown with no lactose and no glucose, its lac genes are:
o: Transcribed at a high level anyway
Silent, because no inducer is present
Transcribed only after lactose is added
e: With no working repressor, nothing blocks the operator, so expression no longer requires lactose (constitutive).
With glucose absent, cAMP–CAP is bound, so transcription is high.
t: Broken repressor (lacI⁻) = always on. CAP still needs low glucose for high-level transcription.

q: The coding region of an mRNA, from the start codon through the stop codon, is 300 nucleotides long. How many amino acids are in the protein?
e: 300 nucleotides ÷ 3 = 100 codons.
The last codon is a stop codon, which doesn't code for an amino acid.
100 − 1 = 99 amino acids (counting the initial Met).

q: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) usually reduce a gene's expression by:
o: Base-pairing with its mRNA to block translation or trigger degradation
Binding its promoter DNA to stop RNA polymerase from starting transcription
Cutting out its introns before the mRNA can leave the nucleus
Adding methyl groups to cytosines in the gene's own promoter DNA
e: A mature miRNA is loaded into the RISC complex.
It pairs (often partly) with sequences in target mRNAs, usually in the 3′ UTR, which represses translation or leads to mRNA breakdown.

q: In eukaryotes, which RNA polymerase transcribes the genes for tRNAs?
e: Pol I makes most rRNA (28S, 18S, 5.8S), Pol II makes mRNA, and Pol III makes tRNA and 5S rRNA.
t: Order by product: I – rRNA, II – mRNA, III – tRNA ('R-M-T').

q: In many eukaryotic promoters, the TATA box about 25–30 bp upstream of the start site is first bound by:
o: RNA polymerase II acting by itself
e: TBP (in TFIID) binds the TATA box and bends the DNA.
Other general transcription factors and RNA polymerase II then assemble on the promoter.

q: In one form of β-thalassemia, a point mutation inside an intron of the β-globin gene creates a new AG splice-acceptor site upstream of the normal one. What is the most likely effect?
o: Part of the intron is kept in the mRNA, often causing a frameshift or early stop
The whole β-globin gene is deleted from the chromosome by the mutation
β-Globin mRNA is made in larger amounts than normal, raising hemoglobin
The intron is removed normally, so the protein's sequence is unchanged
e: Spliceosomes recognize AG at the 3′ end of an intron; a new upstream AG can be used instead of the real one.
The extra intron sequence is retained in the mature mRNA, which usually shifts the reading frame or adds a stop codon, so little normal β-globin is made.

q: How does RNA's sugar differ from DNA's?
o: Ribose has an –OH at the 2′ carbon
e: The 2′-OH makes RNA more reactive and less stable than DNA.

q: What do the 5′ cap and poly-A tail do for eukaryotic mRNA?
o: Protect it from degradation and help with export and translation
Encode the start and stop codons that frame the protein
Mark the intron boundaries for removal by the spliceosome
Anchor the mRNA to its DNA template during transcription
e: Both ends are added during processing in the nucleus.
They stabilize the mRNA, help it leave the nucleus, and help ribosomes bind.

q: An E. coli strain has two lac operons: one on the chromosome with a normal operator, and one on a plasmid with an operator mutation (O<sup>c</sup>) the repressor can't bind. The repressor gene is normal. Without lactose, which lac genes are transcribed?
o: Only those beside the O<sup>c</sup> operator
Both copies, because O<sup>c</sup> inactivates the repressor
Neither copy, because the repressor is normal
Only those beside the normal operator
e: The operator is a DNA site; it controls only the genes on the same DNA molecule (it acts in cis).
Repressor still binds the normal operator, so the chromosomal copy is off; the O<sup>c</sup> copy can't be repressed, so it is on.
t: DNA sites (operators, promoters) act in cis. Diffusible proteins (repressors) act in trans.

q: In anaerobic conditions, why do muscle cells convert pyruvate to lactate?
o: To regenerate NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue
To make extra ATP directly from pyruvate
To regenerate NADH for the electron transport chain
To make glucose in the muscle by gluconeogenesis
e: Glycolysis needs NAD⁺ for the GAPDH step.
Without O₂, NADH can't be reoxidized by the ETC, so lactate dehydrogenase uses NADH to reduce pyruvate, regenerating NAD⁺.

q: Making one glucose from two pyruvates costs how much energy?
e: Pyruvate carboxylase (2 ATP), PEPCK (2 GTP) and phosphoglycerate kinase in reverse (2 ATP) use high-energy phosphates.
2 NADH are used at the GAPDH step.
Gluconeogenesis costs more than glycolysis produces, which is why both can't run at full speed together.

q: Under anaerobic conditions, yeast regenerate NAD⁺ by converting pyruvate into:
e: Pyruvate decarboxylase removes CO₂, giving acetaldehyde.
Alcohol dehydrogenase reduces acetaldehyde to ethanol using NADH, regenerating NAD⁺ for glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase.
Human muscle instead reduces pyruvate directly to lactate, with no CO₂ released.

q: People with G6PD deficiency can develop hemolytic anemia after eating fava beans or taking certain drugs. Why?
o: RBCs make too little NADPH to keep glutathione reduced, so oxidants damage them
RBCs make too little NADH to run glycolysis, so they run out of ATP and lyse
RBCs make too much NADPH, which generates oxidants that damage their membranes
RBCs make too little ribose-5-phosphate to build new hemoglobin molecules
e: Red blood cells rely on the pentose phosphate pathway for NADPH.
NADPH keeps glutathione in its reduced, protective form.
Without it, oxidative stress destroys the cells.

q: During glycogen breakdown, which enzyme removes the α(1→6) branch points?
e: Glycogen phosphorylase only cleaves α(1→4) bonds and stops a few residues from a branch.
Debranching enzyme moves the short chain onto another branch and then hydrolyzes the α(1→6) bond, releasing free glucose.

q: The first step of glycolysis, catalyzed by hexokinase, converts glucose to:
e: Hexokinase uses ATP to phosphorylate glucose at C6.

q: During a long fast, which organ is the main site of gluconeogenesis?
e: Gluconeogenesis builds new glucose from lactate, glycerol and amino acids.
The liver does most of it (the kidney cortex helps during long fasts).
Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so it cannot release free glucose into blood.
t: Liver = the body's glucose bank for everyone else. Muscle keeps glucose for itself.

q: During a fast, glycerol released from adipose triglycerides is used by the liver for gluconeogenesis. At which intermediate does its carbon enter?
e: Liver glycerol kinase makes glycerol-3-phosphate.
Glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase oxidizes it to dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP), a glycolytic/gluconeogenic triose.
Two trioses then combine via aldolase toward glucose.
t: Adipose tissue has little glycerol kinase, so glycerol travels to the liver to be used.

q: What is the net ATP produced by glycolysis per molecule of glucose?
e: Investment phase uses 2 ATP.
Payoff phase makes 4 ATP (plus 2 NADH).
Net = 4 − 2 = 2 ATP
t: Glycolysis happens in the cytosol and needs no O₂.

q: Pyruvate carboxylase, a biotin-dependent mitochondrial enzyme, is allosterically activated by:
e: During fasting, β-oxidation floods the matrix with acetyl-CoA.
Acetyl-CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase (making oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis) and inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase, so pyruvate is saved for glucose.
t: Acetyl-CoA's message: 'Plenty of fuel here: make glucose, don't burn pyruvate.'

q: Gluconeogenesis spans several cell compartments. Which enzyme–location pairing is correct?
e: Pyruvate carboxylase is in the mitochondrial matrix.
Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase is cytosolic, and glucose-6-phosphatase faces the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum.
PEPCK occurs in the matrix and/or cytosol depending on species, never only in the ER.
t: Gluconeogenesis tours the cell: mitochondria → cytosol → ER.

q: ATP is a substrate of PFK-1, yet high ATP levels slow the enzyme. How?
o: ATP also binds an allosteric site that lowers affinity for fructose-6-phosphate
ATP competes with fructose-6-phosphate for the same binding pocket on PFK-1
ATP phosphorylates PFK-1 covalently and inactivates it for hours
ATP is converted to AMP, which then inhibits PFK-1 directly at its active site
e: PFK-1 has two kinds of ATP sites: the catalytic site and a separate inhibitory (allosteric) site.
When ATP is plentiful it fills the allosteric site, shifting the enzyme toward a low-affinity state for fructose-6-phosphate.
AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate reverse this inhibition.

q: One turn of the citric acid cycle (one acetyl-CoA) produces:
e: Per acetyl-CoA: 3 NADH + 1 FADH₂ + 1 GTP (≈ ATP) + 2 CO₂.

q: Which mobile carrier moves electrons from Complex III to Complex IV?
e: Cytochrome c is a small water-soluble heme protein on the intermembrane-space side of the inner membrane.
It carries one electron at a time (Fe³⁺ ⇌ Fe²⁺) from Complex III to Complex IV.
t: Order of carriers: NADH → I → Q → III → cyt c → IV → O₂.

q: Isolated mitochondria are given succinate and Pi, and O₂ use is slow. Adding ADP makes O₂ use jump; it slows again once the ADP has been converted to ATP. What does this show?
o: Electron transport is tightly coupled to ATP synthesis
ADP is the final electron acceptor of the chain
Succinate can't be oxidized until ADP activates Complex II
ADP uncouples mitochondria and lets protons leak in
e: Without ADP, ATP synthase is idle, the proton gradient grows, and pumping (and thus electron flow) is opposed.
ADP lets H⁺ flow through ATP synthase, lowering the gradient, so electrons and O₂ use speed up.
This 'respiratory control' means mitochondria burn fuel only as fast as ATP is needed.

q: Where is ATP synthase located?
e: ATP synthase spans the inner membrane, with its catalytic head facing the matrix.

q: Oligomycin blocks ATP synthase's proton channel. Why does electron transport soon slow down too?
o: The proton gradient builds up until pumping H⁺ becomes too hard
Oligomycin also binds and directly inhibits complex IV
The proton gradient collapses, leaving the pumps nothing to work against
NADH can no longer be made, so complex I runs out of substrate
e: With no H⁺ flowing back through ATP synthase, the gradient gets steeper.
Eventually complexes can't pump against it, so electron flow slows (respiratory control).

q: Which molecule carries electrons from Complexes I and II to Complex III?
e: Ubiquinone is a lipid-soluble carrier in the inner membrane.
Cytochrome c carries electrons from Complex III to Complex IV.

q: Which citric acid cycle step produces GTP (or ATP) by substrate-level phosphorylation?
e: Succinyl-CoA synthetase uses the energy of the thioester bond to make GTP.

q: A person with chronic alcoholism and thiamine (vitamin B₁) deficiency develops lactic acidosis. Why?
o: Pyruvate dehydrogenase can't work, so pyruvate is converted to lactate
Pyruvate carboxylase can't work, so pyruvate is converted to lactate
Lactate dehydrogenase needs thiamine, so lactate can't be reoxidized
Complex IV needs thiamine, so cells switch to anaerobic glycolysis
e: PDH requires thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP).
Without it, pyruvate can't become acetyl-CoA and builds up, and lactate dehydrogenase converts it to lactate.

q: Where does the citric acid cycle take place?
e: All citric acid cycle enzymes are in the matrix except succinate dehydrogenase, which sits in the inner membrane.

q: Which enzyme is the main rate-limiting step of the citric acid cycle?
e: Isocitrate dehydrogenase is activated by ADP and inhibited by ATP and NADH.

q: How many CO₂ molecules are released when one glucose is fully oxidized through pyruvate dehydrogenase and the citric acid cycle?
e: PDH: 1 CO₂ per pyruvate × 2 = 2.
Citric acid cycle: 2 CO₂ per acetyl-CoA × 2 = 4.
Total = 6, accounting for all 6 carbons of glucose.

q: Acetyl-CoA labeled with ¹⁴C at both carbons enters the citric acid cycle. In the first turn, how many of the labeled carbons are released as CO₂?
e: The two CO₂ released in a turn (at isocitrate DH and α-ketoglutarate DH) come from carbons that were in oxaloacetate.
The acetyl carbons stay in the 4-carbon intermediates and become part of the regenerated oxaloacetate; they are released only in later turns.

q: In ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency, carbamoyl phosphate builds up in liver mitochondria and leaks into the cytosol. Which finding results?
o: Orotic acid in the urine, from extra pyrimidine synthesis
Uric acid crystals, from extra purine synthesis
Phenylpyruvate in the urine, from blocked phenylalanine use
High blood citrulline, from faster citrulline synthesis
e: In the cytosol, carbamoyl phosphate is the starting material of pyrimidine synthesis (normally made there by CPS II).
Excess carbamoyl phosphate is pushed into the pathway, and the intermediate orotic acid spills into the urine.
Citrulline is low in OTC deficiency, because OTC is the enzyme that makes it.
t: High ammonia + orotic aciduria + low citrulline → think OTC deficiency.

q: Which lipoprotein carries dietary triglycerides from the intestine to tissues?
e: Chylomicrons: dietary fat from the intestine. VLDL: fat made by the liver. LDL: cholesterol delivery. HDL: cholesterol return to the liver.

q: Before a fatty acid can be oxidized, acyl-CoA synthetase activates it by converting it to:
e: Fatty acid + CoA + ATP → fatty acyl-CoA + AMP + PPi.
PPi hydrolysis makes the step irreversible; the cost counts as 2 ATP equivalents.
Acyl-carnitine forms later, only to cross the inner mitochondrial membrane.

q: Fatty acid synthesis needs acetyl-CoA in the cytosol, but acetyl-CoA is made in mitochondria. How does it get out?
o: It joins oxaloacetate to form citrate, which is exported and cleaved in the cytosol
It diffuses directly through the inner mitochondrial membrane into the cytosol
It is converted to malonyl-CoA, which is then exported to the cytosol
It is converted back to pyruvate, which is exported and then reconverted
e: The inner membrane is impermeable to acetyl-CoA.
Citrate leaves, and ATP-citrate lyase regenerates acetyl-CoA in the cytosol (the citrate shuttle).

q: Where is the urea cycle mainly carried out?
e: Liver cells convert toxic ammonia into urea, which the kidneys excrete.
The cycle's first steps happen in the mitochondria; the rest happens in the cytosol.

q: Beta-oxidation of an even-chain fatty acid primarily yields which two-carbon product?
e: Each beta-oxidation cycle typically removes a two-carbon acetyl-CoA unit.

q: Hormone-sensitive lipase breaks down stored fat. Which hormone inhibits it?
e: Glucagon and epinephrine activate it (through cAMP and PKA) during fasting and stress.
Insulin inhibits it in the fed state, so fat is stored.

q: Where in the cell does β-oxidation of fatty acids occur?
e: Fatty acids are activated (fatty acyl-CoA) in the cytosol.
The carnitine shuttle moves them into the mitochondria.
β-Oxidation happens in the mitochondrial matrix, making acetyl-CoA, NADH and FADH₂.
t: Fatty acid synthesis is in the cytosol; breakdown is in the mitochondria. Opposite places for opposite jobs.

q: Oleate (18:1, cis-Δ9) and stearate (18:0) are each fully oxidized. Using 1.5 ATP per FADH₂, how does oleate's ATP yield compare with stearate's?
o: About 1.5 ATP less, since one FAD-linked step is skipped
About 2.5 ATP less, since one NAD⁺-linked step is skipped
About 10 ATP less, since one acetyl-CoA is lost
The same, since both have 18 carbons in the chain
e: Oleate already has a double bond where acyl-CoA dehydrogenase would normally make one.
An isomerase converts the cis-Δ3 intermediate to trans-Δ2, so that round skips the FADH₂-producing step.
One fewer FADH₂ = about 1.5 fewer ATP; the number of acetyl-CoA and NADH is unchanged.

q: In phenylketonuria (PKU), phenylalanine hydroxylase is deficient. Which amino acid becomes essential for these patients?
e: Normally Phe is converted to Tyr.
Without that enzyme, Tyr must come from the diet, while Phe intake must be restricted.

q: Making one palmitate (16:0) from 8 acetyl-CoA requires how many NADPH?
e: One acetyl-CoA primes the chain; 7 are converted to malonyl-CoA and added, so there are 7 elongation cycles.
Each cycle has two reductions (keto → alcohol, then C=C → C–C), each using one NADPH.
7 × 2 = 14 NADPH.

q: Which enzyme is the rate-limiting step of fatty acid synthesis?
e: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase makes malonyl-CoA (using biotin and ATP).
Insulin and citrate activate it; glucagon inhibits it.

q: Flippases use ATP to:
o: Move phospholipids from one leaflet of the bilayer to the other
Pump Na⁺ out of and K⁺ into the cell across the bilayer
Hydrolyze phospholipids into free fatty acids within the bilayer
Insert newly made proteins into one leaflet of the bilayer
e: Spontaneous flipping is very slow. Flippases maintain the different lipid compositions of the inner and outer leaflets.

q: Cholera toxin keeps intestinal cells' cAMP high, which holds CFTR channels open. Why does this cause massive watery diarrhea?
o: Cl⁻ pours into the gut lumen, and Na⁺ and water follow it
Water is actively pumped by ATP into the gut
e: Open CFTR channels secrete Cl⁻ into the intestine.
Na⁺ follows the negative charge, and water follows the salt by osmosis.
Oral rehydration solution works because SGLT1 (Na⁺–glucose co-transport) still pulls Na⁺ and water back in.

q: Which pair is correctly ordered from MORE permeable to LESS permeable across a pure lipid bilayer?
e: Small, nonpolar or weakly polar molecules cross fastest; large polar molecules and ions cross slowest.
Small ethanol crosses easily; glucose is large and polar. Water, urea and CO₂ all cross better than glucose or ions.

q: The carbohydrate chains of plasma membrane glycoproteins and glycolipids face:
o: The extracellular side of the cell
The cytosolic side of the cell
The hydrophobic core of the bilayer
Both sides of the bilayer equally
e: Sugars are added in the ER and Golgi lumen, which becomes the outside of the cell after vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane.
These sugars form the glycocalyx, used in cell recognition (e.g., ABO blood antigens).

q: Desmosomes give tissues such as skin mechanical strength by linking neighboring cells through cadherins anchored to:
o: Actin filaments of the contractile ring
Collagen fibers in the basement membrane
e: Desmosome cadherins bind each other between cells and attach inside to intermediate filaments (keratin in epithelia).
Hemidesmosomes, by contrast, anchor cells to the basement membrane.

q: A patient with high blood potassium (hyperkalemia) is at risk for heart rhythm problems. How does raising extracellular [K⁺] affect a cardiac cell's resting membrane potential?
o: It becomes less negative (depolarizes), because the K⁺ gradient is smaller
It doesn't change, because the Na⁺/K⁺ pump compensates instantly
e: The resting potential is close to K⁺'s equilibrium potential, E = 61.5 log([K⁺]out/[K⁺]in).
Raising [K⁺]out makes that log less negative.
A partly depolarized cell has fewer recoverable Na⁺ channels, which disrupts normal heart rhythm.

q: Compared with lateral diffusion within one leaflet, spontaneous 'flip-flop' of a phospholipid between leaflets is:
o: Very slow, because the polar head would have to cross the nonpolar core
Very fast, because the polar head is strongly attracted to the nonpolar core
About equally fast, because both depend only on temperature
Impossible, because phospholipids are anchored to membrane proteins
e: Phospholipids swap places with neighbors in their own leaflet millions of times per second.
Moving the charged head through the hydrocarbon core is so unfavorable that unaided flip-flop takes hours to days, which helps keep the two leaflets different.

q: Cells take in LDL particles by binding them to specific receptors in clathrin-coated pits. This is:
e: Receptors concentrate specific cargo into coated pits, which pinch off as vesicles.

q: What is the role of cholesterol in animal cell membranes?
o: It increases fluidity at all temperatures
It decreases fluidity at all temperatures
It forms channels for ion transport
e: At high temperatures, cholesterol restrains phospholipid movement (less fluid).
At low temperatures, it keeps phospholipids from packing tightly (prevents freezing up).
So it acts as a fluidity buffer.
t: Think of cholesterol as the membrane's thermostat.

q: Lipid rafts are small, more ordered membrane patches that cluster certain signaling proteins. They are enriched in:
e: Sphingolipids have long, mostly saturated chains that pack tightly with cholesterol.
This forms thicker, less fluid domains that float within the surrounding bilayer.

q: Small ions such as Na⁺ and K⁺ cross a pure phospholipid bilayer extremely slowly, even though they are smaller than O₂. Why?
o: Shedding their shell of water to enter the nonpolar core costs too much energy
Their positive charge is repelled by the positive fatty acid tails
They are too large to fit between neighboring phospholipids
They bind permanently to the phosphate heads and cannot move
e: In water, an ion is stabilized by a tightly bound hydration shell.
The hydrocarbon core can't replace those interactions, so the energy barrier is huge; ions need channels or carriers.

q: [K⁺] is 5 mM outside a cell and 150 mM inside. Using E = 61.5 log([out]/[in]) mV at 37 °C, what is the K⁺ equilibrium potential?
e: E ≈ −91 mV

q: IgG (about 150 kDa) is two heavy chains and two light chains held by disulfide bonds. On SDS-PAGE with β-mercaptoethanol, which bands appear?
e: β-Mercaptoethanol reduces the disulfide bonds, separating the chains.
Heavy chains run at about 50 kDa and light chains at about 25 kDa.
Without a reducing agent, the intact 150 kDa antibody would run as one band.

q: A mixture of protein P (pI 4.5) and protein Q (pI 10.0) is loaded onto a cation-exchange column (negatively charged beads) at pH 7.0. What happens?
o: P flows through; Q binds until eluted with salt
Q flows through; P binds until eluted with salt
Both bind, because both are charged at pH 7
Neither binds, because the beads are neutral at pH 7
e: At pH 7, P (pI 4.5) is above its pI, so it is negative and is repelled by the negative beads.
Q (pI 10) is below its pI, so it is positive and binds; raising salt later releases it.

q: An activating mutation in Ras prevents it from hydrolyzing its bound GTP. Why does this promote uncontrolled cell growth?
o: Ras stays 'on', signaling for growth without any input
Ras can no longer bind to growth factors at the membrane
Ras is quickly degraded, releasing its growth signal
Ras becomes a kinase that adds phosphates to DNA
e: Ras is active when GTP is bound and turns itself off by hydrolyzing GTP to GDP.
If hydrolysis fails, Ras stays active and keeps the MAP kinase pathway signaling cell division even with no growth factor.
t: Ras is a GTPase switch: GTP = on, GDP = off. Lose the GTPase, lose the off switch.

q: Cyanogen bromide (CNBr) cuts a protein on the carboxyl side of each methionine. How many peptide fragments form from a single-chain protein with three internal Met residues (none at either end)?
e: Each cut adds one fragment to the original one chain.
3 cuts → 3 + 1 = 4 fragments.
t: n internal cuts in one linear chain → n + 1 pieces.

q: Which technique measures a specific protein in a sample by capturing it with antibodies in plastic wells and detecting it with an enzyme-linked antibody that produces a color change?
e: ELISA = enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay.
The amount of colored product is proportional to the amount of antigen captured.

q: Cells are treated with a Gs-coupled receptor agonist that raises cAMP. A second drug then activates a Gi-coupled receptor on the same cells. What happens?
o: cAMP falls because Gαi inhibits adenylyl cyclase
cAMP rises further because Gαi also activates PKA
Ca²⁺ rises because Gαi stimulates phospholipase C
Nothing changes, because Gi needs a receptor tyrosine kinase
e: Gαs stimulates adenylyl cyclase; Gαi inhibits it.
With both active, cyclase activity drops, so cAMP and PKA activity decrease.

q: Which technique separates native proteins primarily by size through a porous matrix?
e: Larger molecules elute earlier because they enter fewer matrix pores.

q: Edman degradation determines a protein's sequence by:
o: Removing and identifying amino acids one at a time from the N-terminus
Cleaving after lysine and arginine and sorting the fragments by mass
Hydrolyzing the whole protein and measuring its amino acid composition
Removing and identifying amino acids one at a time from the C-terminus
e: Phenyl isothiocyanate labels the N-terminal residue, which is then cleaved off and identified.
It works well for short peptides (up to about 50 residues).

q: Many proteins are least soluble in water at a pH equal to their isoelectric point. Why?
o: With no net charge, molecules don't repel and they aggregate
Peptide bonds hydrolyze fastest at the isoelectric point
All side chains are fully protonated at the pI
The protein carries its largest net charge at the pI
e: At the pI, positive and negative charges balance (net 0).
Without like-charge repulsion between molecules, they clump together and precipitate.

q: Which method is best for finding the structure of a small protein while it moves freely in solution?
e: X-ray crystallography needs the protein packed in a crystal.
NMR works on proteins in solution, but mainly for smaller proteins.

q: A ligand-gated ion channel opens when:
o: A specific signaling molecule binds to it
ATP is hydrolyzed by the channel
e: Example: acetylcholine binding the nicotinic receptor at the neuromuscular junction.
Voltage-gated channels respond to voltage; mechanically gated ones respond to stretch.

q: A receptor binds a hormone with K<sub>d</sub> = 4 nM. What fraction of receptors is occupied when the free hormone concentration is 12 nM?
e: Fraction bound = [L]/(K<sub>d</sub> + [L]).

q: A patient feels bloating and gas after drinking milk. Which explanation fits best?
o: Low lactase lets undigested lactose reach colon bacteria, which ferment it
Excess lactase breaks lactose down too fast, flooding the gut with glucose
Milk proteins inhibit pancreatic amylase, so undigested starch reaches the colon
Low sucrase lets undigested sucrose reach the colon, where it is fermented
e: Without enough lactase, lactose can't be split into absorbable monosaccharides.
Colon bacteria ferment it, producing gas and drawing water into the gut (osmotic diarrhea).

q: Glucose is classified as an:
e: Glucose has 6 carbons (hexose) and an aldehyde at C1 (aldo-).

q: Mild oxidation of D-glucose (for example with bromine water) converts only its aldehyde group. Which product forms?
o: Sorbitol, with a new –CH₂OH at C1
Glucaric acid, with –COOH at C1 and C6
e: The aldehyde (C1) is the most easily oxidized group, giving an aldonic acid: gluconic acid.
Oxidizing C6 gives a uronic acid; oxidizing both ends needs stronger conditions; sorbitol is a reduction product.

q: An aldopentose has three chiral carbons in its open-chain form. How many D-aldopentoses are there?
e: Total stereoisomers = 2³ = 8.
Half have the D configuration at the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl: 8/2 = 4 (ribose, arabinose, xylose, lyxose).

q: Which disaccharide is NOT a reducing sugar?
e: A reducing sugar needs a free anomeric carbon that can open into an aldehyde.
In sucrose, both anomeric carbons (glucose C1 and fructose C2) are tied up in the glycosidic bond.

q: In chair conformations, why is β-D-glucopyranose more stable than α-D-glucopyranose?
o: All its –OH and –CH₂OH groups can be equatorial
Its anomeric –OH is axial, away from the ring O
Its ring has fewer atoms, so there is less strain
Its anomeric carbon is not chiral, so it is symmetric
e: In β-D-glucose every large substituent, including the anomeric –OH, sits equatorial.
In α the anomeric –OH is axial, adding steric strain; this is why β is about 64% of the equilibrium mixture.

q: Which bond connects the anomeric carbon of one monosaccharide to another sugar?
e: Glycosidic bonds join carbohydrate units.

q: Benedict's and Tollens' tests detect reducing sugars because these sugars:
o: Have an aldehyde (or can form one) that gets oxidized
Have a ketone group that gets reduced by the reagent
Have a glycosidic bond that the reagent hydrolyzes
Have an aldehyde group that gets reduced to an alcohol
e: The open-chain aldehyde is oxidized to a carboxylic acid.
The reagent is reduced: Cu²⁺ → Cu₂O (red precipitate) or Ag⁺ → Ag (silver mirror).

q: Pure α-D-glucose has a specific rotation of +112°, and pure β-D-glucose +19°. At equilibrium in water the rotation is +53°. About what percentage of the mixture is β?
e: Let x = fraction β: 112(1 − x) + 19x = 53.
t: Check: the equilibrium value is closer to β's rotation, so β must be the majority.

q: A disaccharide made of two glucose units gives a positive Benedict's test. It is hydrolyzed by a β-glucosidase but not by an α-glucosidase. Which disaccharide is it?
e: A β-glucosidase cleaves only β glycosidic bonds, so the link is β.
Positive Benedict's means one anomeric carbon is free; cellobiose fits. Sucrose contains fructose, and trehalose and sucrose are non-reducing.

q: How many stereoisomers are possible for an aldohexose (which has 4 chiral carbons in its open-chain form)?
e: Maximum stereoisomers = 2ⁿ
2⁴ = 16 (8 D-sugars and 8 L-sugars).

q: In sucrose, the fructose unit is present as which kind of ring?
o: It stays as an open chain, not a ring
e: Fructose's C5 –OH attacks its C2 ketone, giving a five-membered ring (four carbons + one O).
In sucrose, fructose's C2 is joined to glucose's C1, locking it as β-fructofuranose.

q: A wax is an ester of:
o: A long-chain fatty acid and a long-chain alcohol
Glycerol and three long-chain fatty acids
Glycerol, two fatty acids and a phosphate
Sphingosine and a long-chain fatty acid
e: Waxes are very hydrophobic and solid at room temperature.
They waterproof leaves, feathers and skin.

q: A lipid extract is boiled with NaOH, then shaken with ether and water. Which lipid ends up in the ether layer chemically unchanged?
e: NaOH hydrolyzes ester bonds (saponification), turning TAGs, glycerophospholipids and waxes into water-soluble carboxylate salts plus alcohols.
Free cholesterol has no ester bond, so it is 'unsaponifiable' and stays nonpolar in the ether layer.

q: Which fatty acid has the highest melting point?
e: Longer chains and fewer double bonds → higher melting point.
Stearic acid is long and fully saturated, so it packs best.

q: Phospholipase C cleaves the membrane lipid PIP₂. Which statement correctly describes the two products?
o: IP₃ diffuses to the ER to release Ca²⁺; DAG stays in the membrane to activate protein kinase C
DAG diffuses to the ER to release Ca²⁺; IP₃ stays in the membrane to activate protein kinase C
IP₃ and DAG both leave the cell and bind receptors on neighboring cells
IP₃ activates adenylyl cyclase, and DAG is stored in fat droplets
e: PIP₂ has a hydrophobic diacylglycerol part and a charged inositol trisphosphate head.
The soluble head (IP₃) moves through the cytosol to open ER Ca²⁺ channels; the hydrophobic DAG stays in the membrane, where it (with Ca²⁺) activates PKC.
t: Think solubility: the charged piece (IP₃) travels; the greasy piece (DAG) stays put.

q: Saponification of a triacylglycerol with NaOH produces:
e: Base hydrolyzes the three ester bonds.
The fatty acids leave as carboxylate salts, which are soaps.

q: A patient with fat malabsorption bruises easily and bleeds longer than normal. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely?
e: Vitamin K is needed to carboxylate (activate) several clotting factors.
Fat malabsorption reduces uptake of fat-soluble vitamins.

q: A patient receives fat-free intravenous nutrition for several weeks and develops scaly dermatitis and poor wound healing. Adding which lipid would most likely correct this?
e: Human desaturases cannot add double bonds beyond C9 (from the carboxyl end), so we cannot make linoleic (ω-6) or α-linolenic (ω-3) acid.
These essential fatty acids must come from the diet; the others listed can be made by the body.
t: Essential fatty acids: linoleic and α-linolenic. Oleic acid is NOT essential.

q: A child lacks lipoprotein lipase, the capillary-wall enzyme that hydrolyzes triacylglycerols carried in blood lipoproteins. After a fatty meal, which change is expected?
o: Chylomicrons build up in the blood, making the plasma look milky
Dietary fat stays undigested in the gut and appears in the stool
Blood LDL falls to near zero because LDL receptors are missing
Adipose tissue takes up more fatty acids than normal
e: Lipoprotein lipase releases fatty acids from chylomicron and VLDL triacylglycerols so that muscle and adipose tissue can take them up.
Without it, triacylglycerol-rich chylomicrons can't be cleared, so plasma triacylglycerol soars and the plasma looks milky (lipemic). Digestion in the gut by pancreatic lipase is normal.

q: In a glycerophospholipid, glycerol carbons 1 and 2 carry fatty acids. What is attached to carbon 3?
o: A phosphate linked to a polar head group
A third fatty acid joined by an ester
A sphingosine chain joined by an amide
A single sugar joined by a glycosidic bond
e: Glycerophospholipids are built on glycerol-3-phosphate.
C1 and C2 carry fatty acyl chains; C3 carries a phosphate that is usually linked to a head group such as choline, serine or ethanolamine.
A third fatty acid on C3 would make a triacylglycerol instead.

q: Why do cis double bonds lower a fatty acid's melting point?
o: They create kinks that keep chains from packing tightly
They lengthen the chains, reducing van der Waals contact
They add hydrogen bonds that disrupt chain packing
They make the carboxyl group more ionized and soluble
e: Tightly packed chains have strong dispersion forces.
Kinks disrupt packing, weakening those forces, so the fat melts at a lower temperature (oils are liquid).

q: At pH 7.4, which membrane phospholipid carries a net negative charge?
e: Phosphatidylserine: phosphate (−1) + serine carboxylate (−1) + serine amine (+1) = net −1.
Phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidylethanolamine and sphingomyelin each pair a −1 phosphate with a +1 head group, giving net 0.
t: PS = Phosphatidyl-Serine = the Sour (negative) one; it has the extra carboxylate.

q: Why are fat-soluble vitamins more likely than water-soluble vitamins to reach toxic levels when taken in large doses?
o: They are stored in liver and fat instead of being excreted in urine
They are absorbed directly into the blood without any regulation
They are broken down by the liver into more toxic water-soluble forms
They bind tightly to hemoglobin and block oxygen transport
e: Excess water-soluble vitamins (B, C) are largely cleared by the kidneys.
Vitamins A, D, E and K dissolve in lipid stores and accumulate, so megadoses (especially of A and D) can be toxic.

q: During the first few seconds of intense exercise, muscle quickly regenerates ATP using:
e: Creatine kinase transfers a phosphate from phosphocreatine to ADP.
It's the fastest backup, lasting only about 10 seconds.

q: Complete oxidation of glucose has ΔG°′ ≈ −2870 kJ mol⁻¹. If it yields 32 ATP (ΔG°′ = +30.5 kJ mol⁻¹ each), about what fraction of the energy is captured as ATP under standard conditions?
e: Energy stored = 32 × 30.5 ≈ 976 kJ.
Efficiency = 976 ÷ 2870 ≈ 0.34, or about 34%; the rest is released as heat.
t: Under real cell conditions ATP's ΔG is larger, so true efficiency is higher than this estimate.

q: Metabolic pathways are usually regulated at enzymes whose reactions are far from equilibrium. Why?
o: Their large negative ΔG means changing their activity changes pathway flux
Near-equilibrium enzymes are too slow to affect pathway flux at all
Far-from-equilibrium steps are easily reversed by mass action
Enzymes near equilibrium can't bind allosteric effectors
e: A near-equilibrium step runs both ways quickly; its net direction simply follows substrate and product levels.
A far-from-equilibrium step (ΔG ≪ 0) is effectively one-way and often slow, so it limits flux; speeding it up or slowing it down controls the whole pathway.
Examples: hexokinase, PFK-1, pyruvate kinase, isocitrate dehydrogenase.

q: During a long fast, the body's fuel sources change over time. Which order is correct?
o: Liver glycogen → gluconeogenesis rises → ketone bodies become major fuel
Ketone bodies → liver glycogen is used → gluconeogenesis rises
Muscle protein → liver glycogen → fat stores become major fuel
Liver glycogen → ketone bodies become major fuel → gluconeogenesis rises
e: Liver glycogen lasts roughly a day.
Gluconeogenesis rises (from amino acids, lactate, glycerol).
After several days, ketone bodies from fat become a major fuel, sparing protein.

q: Cells build highly ordered macromolecules from simpler molecules. Why doesn't this violate the second law of thermodynamics?
o: Cells release heat and small molecules, raising total entropy
Living cells are isolated systems that are exempt from the law
Enzymes directly lower the total entropy of the universe
Building macromolecules raises entropy inside the cell itself
e: Cells are open systems that exchange matter and energy with their surroundings.
Breaking down fuels to CO₂ and H₂O and giving off heat increases the surroundings' entropy more than biosynthesis decreases the cell's.
So the entropy of cell + surroundings still increases.

q: In prolonged starvation, the rate of muscle protein breakdown falls after the first week or so. What best explains this?
o: The brain switches largely to ketone bodies, so less glucose must be made
Liver glycogen is rebuilt and once again supplies most blood glucose
Muscle begins making glucose from its own stored fatty acids
Insulin rises during starvation and blocks muscle protein breakdown
e: Early in a fast, gluconeogenesis from amino acids (from muscle protein) supplies the brain's glucose.
As ketone bodies rise, the brain gets a large share of its energy from them, so glucose demand and amino-acid use drop.
This protein sparing preserves muscle; fatty acids can't be made into net glucose.

q: During a 'fight or flight' response, epinephrine causes:
o: Glycogen breakdown in liver and muscle
Glycogen synthesis in liver and muscle
Lower heart rate and slower breathing
More insulin release from the pancreas
e: Epinephrine activates cAMP signaling, mobilizing glucose and fatty acids for quick energy.

q: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, which process does insulin promote?
o: Glycogen synthesis in liver and muscle
e: Insulin turns on storage: glycogen synthesis, fatty acid synthesis and GLUT4-mediated glucose uptake.

q: When NAD⁺ is converted to NADH during a dehydrogenase reaction, NAD⁺ is:
o: Reduced, accepting a single proton only
e: The substrate loses two electrons and two H atoms.
NAD⁺ takes one H as a hydride ion (2 e⁻ + H⁺); the other H⁺ goes into solution.
Gaining electrons is reduction.
t: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

q: Adenylate kinase keeps 2 ADP ⇌ ATP + AMP near equilibrium. Why does this make AMP a sensitive signal of low cellular energy?
o: A small drop in ATP causes a much larger relative rise in AMP
AMP is made only once ATP has been completely used up
AMP directly inhibits adenylate kinase whenever ATP falls
AMP stays nearly constant while ADP rises sharply instead
e: With K ≈ 1, [AMP] ≈ [ADP]² ÷ [ATP].
Example: ATP 4.8 mM, ADP 0.2 mM → AMP ≈ 0.008 mM. If ATP falls to 4.5 mM and ADP rises to 0.4 mM → AMP ≈ 0.036 mM.
ATP fell ~6%, but AMP rose ~4-fold, so AMP-sensing enzymes (PFK-1, glycogen phosphorylase, AMPK) respond strongly.

q: Which carrier mainly supplies electrons for biosynthetic (reductive) reactions such as fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis?
e: Cells keep NADPH/NADP⁺ high, ready to donate electrons for building molecules.
NADH/NAD⁺ is kept mostly oxidized for catabolism, sending electrons to the ETC. ATP carries energy, not electrons.
t: P for 'production' (biosynthesis): NADPH builds, NADH burns.

q: Under standard biochemical conditions, ATP hydrolysis to ADP + Pi releases about:
e: ΔG°′ ≈ −30.5 kJ mol⁻¹ (about −7.3 kcal mol⁻¹).
In real cells, ΔG is even more negative (about −50 kJ mol⁻¹) because of actual concentrations.

q: The titration curve of glycine is shown. What is glycine's isoelectric point?
e: It's the point after 1 equivalent of OH⁻.

q: Long-chain fatty acyl groups cross the inner mitochondrial membrane while attached to compound X (shown). What is compound X?
e: Carnitine acyltransferase I moves the acyl group from CoA to carnitine on the outer side.
A translocase carries acyl-carnitine across; carnitine acyltransferase II puts the acyl group back on CoA in the matrix.
t: Choline also has a trimethylammonium group but no carboxylate; don't confuse the two.

Numbering from the carboxyl carbon (C1), the double bond starts at C9, so Δ⁹.
Both chain segments are on the same side of the double bond, so it is cis (this is palmitoleic acid, an ω-7).

q: An experiment measures product formed in 10 minutes at three substrate concentrations (shown). What best explains why quadrupling [S] from 4 to 16 mM increases product less than quadrupling it from 1 to 4 mM?
o: The enzyme was denatured at 16 mM
The reaction became zero order at 1 mM
e: At higher [S], more active sites are occupied, so the rate rises less (Michaelis–Menten).
