q: Bird wings and insect wings evolved separately to solve the same problem. This is an example of:
e: Similar environments can select for similar features in unrelated organisms.

q: Two genes are 10 map units apart. About what percentage of offspring are recombinant?
e: 1 map unit (centimorgan) = 1% recombination frequency.

q: Human birth weight shows that very small and very large babies have lower survival, while medium weights do best. This is:
e: Selection favors the middle and acts against both extremes.

q: Genetic drift has the biggest effect in:
e: Random chance changes allele frequencies more in small groups.

q: Two genes located close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together. This is:
e: Close genes are rarely separated by crossing over, so they don't assort independently.

q: Structures that look different but share a common evolutionary origin, like a human arm and a bat wing, are:
e: Analogous structures (like bird and insect wings) have similar function but different origins.

q: In a population in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, 16% of people show a recessive trait. What fraction are heterozygous carriers?
e: Recessive phenotype = q² = 0.16, so q = 0.4.
t: Always start from q² (the recessive phenotype). It's the only genotype you can see directly.

q: A man and a woman are both unaffected, and each has a sibling with the same autosomal recessive disease. All four of their parents are unaffected. What is the probability that their first child will be affected?
e: Each unaffected person whose parents are both carriers has a 2/3 chance of being a carrier (AA : Aa : aa = 1 : 2 : 1, excluding aa).
Both must be carriers and the child must get two recessive alleles: 2/3 × 2/3 × 1/4 = 4/36 = 1/9
t: Once you know someone is unaffected, use 2/3, not 1/2, for their carrier chance.

q: A woman who is a carrier of an X-linked recessive disorder has children with an unaffected man. What is the probability that a son will be affected?
e: Mother: XᴬXᵃ. Father: XᴬY.
A son always gets Y from dad and one X from mom.
Mom passes Xᵃ half the time, so P(affected son) = ½.
t: Read carefully: 'probability a son is affected' (½) differs from 'probability a child is an affected son' (¼).

q: A man with red–green color blindness (X-linked recessive) has children with a woman who has two normal alleles. Which statement about their children is correct?
o: All daughters are carriers, and no sons are affected
Half of the daughters are carriers, and half of the sons are affected
All sons are affected, and no daughters are carriers
No daughters are carriers, and all sons are carriers
e: The father gives his only X (with the allele) to every daughter, and his Y to every son.
Daughters get one normal X from the mother, so all are carriers; sons get the mother's normal X, so none are affected.

q: A fly heterozygous for two linked genes (AB on one chromosome, ab on the other) is test-crossed to an aabb fly. The 1000 offspring are: 420 AB, 430 ab, 70 Ab and 80 aB. How far apart are the genes?
e: Recombinant offspring are the new combinations: Ab + aB = 70 + 80 = 150.
Recombination frequency = 150 ÷ 1000 = 0.15 = 15%, which is 15 map units (centimorgans).
t: The two biggest classes are the parental types; the two smallest are recombinants.

q: An organism with two different alleles for a gene is:
e: Hetero = different.

q: A bacterial population doubles every 20 minutes. Starting with 100 cells under ideal conditions, how many are there after 2 hours?
e: 2 hours = 120 min = 6 doublings.

q: Peroxisomes break down very long-chain fatty acids and also:
o: Break down hydrogen peroxide using catalase
e: Peroxisome reactions make H₂O₂; catalase converts it to water and O₂.

q: If a few lysosomal hydrolases leak into the cytosol, they usually cause little damage. What is the best explanation?
o: They work best near pH 5, but the cytosol is near pH 7.2
The cytosol contains no proteins or lipids to digest
They stay inactive until tagged with mannose-6-phosphate
They need ATP, which is absent from the cytosol
e: Lysosomal enzymes are acid hydrolases; a proton pump keeps the lysosome lumen at about pH 5.
At the neutral pH of the cytosol, these enzymes are much less active, which protects the cell from small leaks.
Mannose-6-phosphate is a sorting tag, not an activation switch.

q: Which statement best describes a bacterial plasmid?
o: A small circular DNA that replicates on its own
A protein coat that shields the chromosome
A short RNA strand that guides the cell's division
A membrane sac that stores extra ribosomes
e: Plasmids are extrachromosomal DNA circles with their own origin of replication.
They are not essential for survival but often carry useful genes, such as antibiotic resistance.

q: How does bacterial binary fission differ from eukaryotic mitosis?
o: It occurs with no spindle and no nuclear envelope
It produces two genetically different cells
It requires homologous chromosomes to pair up
It occurs only after a round of conjugation
e: Bacteria have no nucleus and no mitotic spindle. The single circular chromosome is copied and the two copies are moved apart as the cell grows and pinches in two.
Like mitosis, it produces two genetically identical cells (barring mutations).

q: Antibiotic resistance is rising. Why does finishing a full course of antibiotics, rather than stopping early, help limit resistance?
o: It kills the less-susceptible survivors that would otherwise multiply
It prevents the antibiotic from inducing new resistance mutations
It boosts the patient's immune cells so they clear the bacteria
It lets the drug kill bacteria that are already fully resistant
e: Stopping early can leave the toughest bacteria alive.
They then multiply, shifting the population toward resistance: natural selection in action.

q: Gram-positive bacteria stain purple in a Gram stain because they have:
o: A thick peptidoglycan wall that retains crystal violet
An outer membrane rich in lipopolysaccharide
A waxy mycolic acid layer that traps the dye
A thin peptidoglycan layer between two membranes
e: The thick peptidoglycan traps the dye.
Gram-negative bacteria have a thin wall plus an outer membrane, so they lose the dye and stain pink.

q: A cube-shaped cell doubles its edge length. How does its surface-area-to-volume ratio change?
e: Surface area scales with length²: 2² = 4 times larger. Volume scales with length³: 2³ = 8 times larger.
New ratio = 4/8 = ½ of the original.
t: This is why cells stay small: volume (needs) outgrows surface (supply).

q: Which statement is true of prokaryotic cells?
o: Their DNA is in a nucleoid region
e: Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles, including a nucleus.
Their circular chromosome sits in the nucleoid region.
They have 70S ribosomes (eukaryotic cytosolic ribosomes are 80S).
t: Many antibiotics target 70S ribosomes, which is why they can kill bacteria without killing you.

q: Which structure is present in typical bacteria but absent from animal cells?
e: Most bacteria have cell walls containing peptidoglycan.

q: In a tube of thioglycolate broth, O₂ is highest at the top and falls to almost zero at the bottom. A bacterium grows only in a band at the very bottom. It is most likely:
e: Obligate aerobes grow only at the top; facultative anaerobes grow throughout but best near the top.
Aerotolerant anaerobes ignore O₂ and grow evenly.
Growth only where O₂ is absent means O₂ is toxic to the cell: an obligate anaerobe.

q: In I-cell disease, cells cannot add mannose-6-phosphate to newly made lysosomal enzymes. What happens to these enzymes?
o: They are secreted instead of reaching lysosomes
They are kept in the nucleus instead of lysosomes
They are sent into mitochondria instead of lysosomes
They are degraded on free ribosomes as they are made
e: In the Golgi, the mannose-6-phosphate tag is recognized by receptors that send enzymes to lysosomes.
Without the tag, the enzymes follow the default secretory path out of the cell, so blood levels rise while lysosomes fill with undigested material.

q: At birth, a human female's primary oocytes are arrested in:
e: Primary oocytes pause in prophase I from before birth; starting at puberty, one resumes meiosis I each cycle just before ovulation, so some stay arrested for decades.
At ovulation, the secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase II and finishes meiosis only if fertilized.

q: Which event happens in meiosis I but not in mitosis?
o: Homologous chromosomes pair up and separate
e: Synapsis (pairing of homologs) and crossing over happen in prophase I.
In anaphase I, homologs (not sister chromatids) separate.

q: At which structure do spindle microtubules attach to a chromosome?
o: The telomere at each chromosome end
e: Each sister chromatid has a kinetochore, a protein complex built on the centromere.
Spindle microtubules bind kinetochores and use them to pull chromatids toward the poles.

q: In which phase of mitosis do sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles?
e: Anaphase: cohesin is cut and chromatids are pulled apart.
Metaphase: chromosomes line up at the middle.

q: If no embryo implants, what most directly triggers menstruation at the end of the ovarian cycle?
o: Progesterone falls as the corpus luteum breaks down
Estrogen rises sharply as new follicles mature
An LH surge causes the lining to detach
hCG rises and breaks down the endometrium
e: Without hCG from an embryo, the corpus luteum degenerates about 2 weeks after ovulation.
Progesterone (and estrogen) levels drop, the endometrium loses its hormonal support, and the lining is shed.

q: Down syndrome risk rises with maternal age. Based on oogenesis, which explanation is most reasonable?
o: Oocytes arrest in meiosis for decades, so nondisjunction is likelier when it resumes
Older women make new oocytes by mitosis, and these are more error-prone
Older mothers' embryos divide more slowly by mitosis, causing chromosome loss
Aging oocytes accumulate point mutations in genes on chromosome 21
e: All primary oocytes form before birth and pause in prophase I.
The longer the pause, the more likely chromosome separation errors become.

q: A human secondary oocyte is ovulated while arrested in metaphase II. When does it complete meiosis II?
o: Only if a sperm fertilizes it
e: The LH surge lets the primary oocyte finish meiosis I just before ovulation; the resulting secondary oocyte then stops at metaphase II.
Sperm entry triggers completion of meiosis II, producing the mature ovum and a second polar body. Without fertilization, meiosis II is never finished.

q: After leaving the seminiferous tubules, where do sperm mature and gain the ability to swim?
e: Sperm made in the seminiferous tubules are not yet motile.
They mature and are stored in the epididymis, then travel through the vas deferens during ejaculation.
t: Sperm route: seminiferous tubules → epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct → urethra.

q: Nondisjunction of one chromosome pair occurs in meiosis I of a primary spermatocyte; meiosis II is normal. How many of the four resulting sperm have an abnormal number of that chromosome?
e: In meiosis I, both homologs go to one secondary spermatocyte and none go to the other.
Meiosis II then gives two n + 1 sperm from one cell and two n − 1 sperm from the other: 4 of 4 abnormal.
(A meiosis II error gives 2 normal, 1 n + 1 and 1 n − 1.)
t: Error in meiosis I: all four gametes are affected. Error in meiosis II: only half.

q: After ovulation, the corpus luteum mainly secretes:
e: Progesterone keeps the uterine lining ready for implantation.
If no pregnancy occurs, the corpus luteum breaks down and menstruation follows.

q: Sertoli cells in the testes:
o: Secrete testosterone in response to LH
e: Sertoli cells (stimulated by FSH) nurse developing sperm.
Leydig cells (stimulated by LH) make testosterone.

q: During which phase of meiosis does crossing over occur?
e: Homologous chromosomes pair up (synapsis) in prophase I.
Non-sister chromatids exchange segments at chiasmata.
This shuffles alleles and increases genetic variation.
t: Crossing over only happens between homologs, and homologs only pair in meiosis I.

q: In somatic cell nuclear transfer, a nucleus from an adult sheep's udder cell was placed into an egg whose own nucleus had been removed, and a whole lamb developed. What does this show about differentiated cells?
o: Their nuclei still hold the genes needed for a whole body
Differentiation is caused by a permanent loss of many genes
Udder cells are totipotent while inside the adult body
Only DNA from an egg nucleus can direct development
e: A complete animal developed from an adult cell's nucleus, so no genes needed for development had been lost.
Differentiation is therefore mostly reversible gene regulation, which the egg cytoplasm was able to reset.

q: An infant has severe constipation because one segment of the colon lacks the nerve cells normally found in its wall. Failed migration of which embryonic cells best explains this?
e: The enteric nervous system (the gut's own neurons) is built from neural crest cells that migrate along the gut.
If they fail to reach the end of the colon, that segment cannot push stool along (Hirschsprung disease).

q: Which germ layer forms skeletal muscle, bone, blood and the kidneys?
e: Mesoderm forms the 'middle' tissues: muscle, bone, connective tissue, the heart and blood, kidneys and gonads.

q: A zygote completes four rounds of cleavage with no growth. Compared with the zygote, about what volume does each cell have?
e: Four doublings give 2⁴ = 16 cells.
With no growth, the zygote's volume is shared 16 ways, so each cell has about 1/16 of it.

q: A solid ball of cells formed by early cleavage divisions is called a:
e: Zygote → morula (solid ball) → blastula/blastocyst (hollow) → gastrula (three germ layers).

q: Why does fetal hemoglobin (HbF) help the fetus get oxygen from the mother?
o: HbF binds O₂ more tightly than adult hemoglobin
HbF binds O₂ less tightly than adult hemoglobin
HbF binds 2,3-BPG more strongly than adult hemoglobin
HbF has more heme groups per molecule than HbA
e: HbF binds 2,3-BPG poorly, so its O₂ curve is left-shifted.
O₂ moves from maternal hemoglobin to fetal hemoglobin across the placenta.

q: A drug taken in the first trimester causes limb malformations, but the same dose in the third trimester does not. What best explains this?
o: Limbs and organs form in the first trimester, the period most sensitive to teratogens
The placenta forms only in the third trimester, so early drugs reach the fetus freely
The fetus has no circulation in the first trimester, so drugs accumulate in tissues
Drugs can't cross the placenta in the third trimester, so the fetus is unexposed
e: Organogenesis happens mostly in weeks 3–8.
This is when teratogens (like thalidomide) cause major structural defects.

q: In the fetus, the ductus arteriosus allows blood to:
o: Bypass the lungs, flowing from pulmonary artery to aorta
Bypass the liver, flowing from umbilical vein to vena cava
Bypass the lungs, flowing from right atrium to left atrium
Return oxygenated blood from the placenta to the heart
e: Fetal lungs aren't used for gas exchange.
Foramen ovale: right atrium → left atrium. Ductus venosus: bypasses the liver.

q: Fertilization usually occurs in the:
e: The egg is fertilized in the ampulla of the fallopian tube, then travels to the uterus.

q: If the anterior (head) end of the neural tube fails to close, which condition results?
e: The front of the neural tube becomes the brain; failure to close there means the brain and skull do not form properly.
Failure at the posterior (tail) end gives spina bifida.
t: Head end open → anencephaly; tail end open → spina bifida.

q: Cells becoming committed to a particular fate, even before they look different, is called:
e: Determination is commitment to a fate.
Differentiation is the later process of becoming specialized in structure and function.

q: Folic acid before and during early pregnancy mainly helps prevent:
o: Neural tube defects like spina bifida
e: Folate is needed for DNA synthesis during rapid cell division.
The neural tube closes in about the 4th week, often before a woman knows she's pregnant.

q: The rapid depolarization (rising phase) of an action potential is caused by:
e: At threshold, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open.
Na⁺ rushes in down its electrochemical gradient.
The inside quickly becomes positive. Repolarization then comes from K⁺ flowing out.
t: Na⁺ in = up. K⁺ out = down.

q: Two subthreshold signals arrive at the same synapse in quick succession and together reach threshold. This is:
e: Temporal summation: repeated inputs from one source, close in time.
Spatial summation: inputs from several sources at once.

q: Which cells make myelin in the central nervous system?
e: CNS: oligodendrocytes. PNS: Schwann cells.

q: How does a sensory neuron signal that a touch has become stronger?
o: It fires action potentials more often
Its action potentials last much longer
It reverses the direction of its signal
e: Action potentials are all-or-none, so their size cannot code strength.
A stronger stimulus raises the firing frequency (and recruits more neurons).

q: A neuron rests at −70 mV with a threshold of −55 mV. At the same moment, its axon hillock receives three EPSPs of +6 mV each and one IPSP of −4 mV. Assuming the potentials simply add, what happens?
o: It reaches −56 mV and does not fire
It reaches −60 mV and does not fire
e: Net change = 3(+6) + (−4) = +14 mV.
−70 + 14 = −56 mV, which is still 1 mV short of the −55 mV threshold, so no action potential.
t: −52 mV forgets the IPSP; −48 mV adds it in the wrong direction.

q: Which brain region is the main center for coordinating balance and fine movement?
e: The cerebellum compares intended movements with actual movement and corrects errors.

q: Cells in the carotid bodies detect a drop in blood O₂ and signal the brainstem to increase breathing. These receptors are best classified as:
e: Chemoreceptors respond to chemical concentrations, here O₂ (as well as CO₂ and H⁺).
Mechanoreceptors sense stretch or pressure, nociceptors sense harmful stimuli, and thermoreceptors sense temperature.

q: Which brain structure is most important for forming new long-term explicit memories?
e: Damage to the hippocampus causes anterograde amnesia: trouble forming new memories.

q: Local anesthetics block pain without making a patient unconscious. Based on how they act, where do they work?
o: On voltage-gated Na⁺ channels in local nerve fibers, blocking conduction
On GABA receptors in the brain, dampening conscious awareness of pain
On voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels in muscle, preventing contraction
On opioid receptors in the spinal cord, inhibiting pain transmission
e: They stop action potentials from traveling in nerves near the injection site.
Pain signals never reach the brain.

q: Parasympathetic stimulation of the heart:
e: The vagus nerve releases ACh at the SA node, slowing it down.

q: A drug blocks acetylcholinesterase. What happens at the neuromuscular junction?
o: Acetylcholine stays in the synapse longer, prolonging muscle stimulation
Acetylcholine release stops, so the muscle can't be stimulated
Acetylcholine receptors are blocked, so the muscle is paralyzed
Acetylcholine is broken down faster, shortening muscle stimulation
e: Acetylcholinesterase normally breaks down ACh quickly.
Blocking it prolongs ACh action (the basis of some nerve agents and myasthenia gravis treatments).

q: Sweating is controlled by the sympathetic nervous system, yet atropine, which blocks muscarinic ACh receptors, reduces sweating. Why?
o: Sympathetic fibers to sweat glands release ACh
Sweat glands are under parasympathetic control
Atropine destroys sweat gland cells directly
e: Sweat glands are an exception: their sympathetic postganglionic fibers are cholinergic.
They release ACh onto muscarinic receptors, so a muscarinic blocker like atropine reduces sweating.

q: Cells exposed to chronically high insulin levels reduce the number of insulin receptors on their surface. What is the result?
o: Cells respond less to the same insulin level
Cells respond more to the same insulin level
Insulin starts entering cells to act on DNA
Glucagon starts binding the insulin receptors
e: Fewer receptors means fewer hormone–receptor complexes at any given insulin level.
This down-regulation lowers sensitivity and is one contributor to insulin resistance.

q: Somatostatin released by pancreatic δ (delta) cells:
o: Inhibits the release of both insulin and glucagon
Stimulates insulin release but blocks glucagon release
Raises blood glucose by breaking down liver glycogen
Stimulates the release of pancreatic digestive enzymes
e: Somatostatin is a broad 'brake' hormone: within the islets it acts locally to suppress both α and β cells.
It also inhibits growth hormone release and many digestive secretions.

q: Thyroid hormone is unusual because it is made from tyrosine yet acts like a steroid. How?
o: It enters cells and binds nuclear receptors that change gene expression
It binds cell-surface GPCRs that raise intracellular cAMP
It is converted to cholesterol before entering target cells
It binds receptor tyrosine kinases that phosphorylate target proteins in the cytoplasm
e: Thyroid hormones are lipid-soluble enough to enter cells.
They change gene transcription, increasing metabolic rate.

q: A tumor of the adrenal medulla releases bursts of hormone. During an episode, which signs are most likely?
o: Fast heartbeat, sweating and high blood pressure
Slow heartbeat, drowsiness and low blood pressure
Weight gain, cold intolerance and dry skin
Low blood glucose, small pupils and low pressure
e: The adrenal medulla secretes epinephrine and norepinephrine.
A burst of catecholamines produces a 'fight or flight' state: fast, forceful heartbeat, vasoconstriction (high BP), sweating, and higher glucose.

q: Peptide hormones usually act within seconds to minutes, while steroid hormones often take hours. Why?
o: Peptides alter existing proteins; steroids alter transcription
Peptides diffuse through the cell membrane faster than steroids
Steroids are broken down in the blood before they can act
Steroids must first be converted into peptides inside cells
e: Peptide hormones bind surface receptors; second messengers quickly activate or inhibit proteins already in the cell.
Steroids bind intracellular receptors that act on DNA, so new mRNA and protein must be made, which takes hours.

q: A bodybuilder injects large doses of testosterone for months. What happens to his own LH secretion and his sperm production?
o: LH falls and sperm production drops
LH rises and sperm production increases
LH falls but sperm production increases
LH rises but sperm production drops
e: Excess androgen feeds back on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, lowering GnRH, LH and FSH.
Spermatogenesis needs FSH and high testosterone made inside the testes, so the testes shrink and sperm counts fall.

q: A head injury cuts the pituitary stalk, so hypothalamic signals no longer reach the anterior pituitary. Which anterior pituitary hormone is most likely to RISE?
e: Most anterior pituitary hormones need stimulating releasing hormones (CRH, TRH, GHRH), so they fall.
Prolactin is mainly held down by dopamine from the hypothalamus; losing this inhibition lets prolactin rise.
t: Prolactin is the pituitary hormone on a leash: cut the leash (dopamine) and it goes up.

q: Iodine deficiency can cause a goiter (enlarged thyroid). Why?
o: Too little thyroid hormone raises TSH, which overstimulates the thyroid
Iodine shortage makes thyroid cells inflame and swell from damage
TSH falls to zero, so the gland swells with unused colloid
The thyroid hoards extra iodine, which expands the follicles
e: Thyroid hormone needs iodine.
Low hormone → high TSH → thyroid growth.

q: A pituitary tumor begins secreting excess growth hormone in a 40-year-old man. His hands, feet and jaw slowly enlarge, but he does not grow taller. Why?
o: His growth plates have fused, so long bones can't lengthen
Growth hormone acts only on the bones of the hands and face
Excess growth hormone blocks IGF-1 production by the liver
Adults lack growth hormone receptors on their bone cells
e: Growth hormone, acting largely through IGF-1 from the liver, stimulates bone and soft-tissue growth.
After puberty the epiphyseal plates have fused, so bones can only thicken and soft tissues enlarge (acromegaly); before fusion the same tumor causes gigantism.
t: GH excess before the plates close → gigantism; after → acromegaly.

q: Which gland secretes melatonin?
e: Melatonin rises in darkness and helps regulate the sleep–wake cycle.

q: Growth hormone promotes growth partly by stimulating the liver to make:
e: IGF-1 drives bone and muscle growth.

q: Which gland is often called the 'master gland' because it controls other endocrine glands?
e: It releases tropic hormones (TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH) that control other glands. The hypothalamus controls it in turn.

q: At rest, normal exhalation is mainly caused by:
o: Passive elastic recoil of the stretched lungs
Active contraction of the diaphragm upward
Contraction of the external intercostal muscles
Strong contraction of the abdominal muscles
e: During quiet breathing, the diaphragm simply relaxes and the stretched lungs recoil, pushing air out.
Abdominal and internal intercostal muscles are used only for forced exhalation; external intercostals help inhalation.
t: The diaphragm never pushes up actively: it contracts (down) to inhale and relaxes to exhale.

q: Most CO₂ is carried in the blood as:
o: CO₂ bound to iron in hemoglobin
e: Carbonic anhydrase in red blood cells converts CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻.
About 70% of CO₂ travels this way.

q: Where does gas exchange occur in the lungs?
e: Alveoli have thin walls and a huge surface area, surrounded by capillaries.

q: A patient with COPD has chronically high CO₂. Why might giving too much O₂ be risky?
o: Extra O₂ worsens V/Q matching and lowers Hb's CO₂ binding, raising CO₂
Extra O₂ causes metabolic alkalosis by lowering blood H⁺
Extra O₂ blocks hemoglobin's heme sites like carbon monoxide
Extra O₂ causes excess surfactant to flood the alveoli
e: Giving high-flow O₂ to some COPD patients can raise CO₂ further.
Current evidence points mainly to worse ventilation–perfusion matching (O₂ reverses protective vasoconstriction in poorly ventilated lung) and the Haldane effect (oxygenated Hb carries less CO₂).
The older 'loss of hypoxic drive' explanation plays a smaller role. Clinicians target a moderate O₂ saturation (about 88–92%).

q: A patient with emphysema has damaged alveolar walls. Which change best explains their trouble with gas exchange?
o: Less alveolar surface area for diffusion
e: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls, merging them into larger, fewer air spaces.

q: At sea level (760 mmHg), air is 21% O₂. What is the partial pressure of O₂ in dry air?
A patient breathes rapidly during a panic attack and feels tingling in the fingers. What is happening to the blood?
o: CO₂ falls and pH rises (respiratory alkalosis)
CO₂ rises and pH falls (respiratory acidosis)
HCO₃⁻ falls and pH falls (metabolic acidosis)
HCO₃⁻ rises and pH rises (metabolic alkalosis)
e: Over-breathing blows off CO₂, shifting the bicarbonate equilibrium left and raising pH.
Alkalosis lowers free Ca²⁺, causing tingling.

q: Early lung disease that thickens the alveolar membrane often lowers arterial P(O₂) while P(CO₂) stays near normal. Why?
o: CO₂ is far more soluble, so it diffuses faster
CO₂ is a smaller molecule that slips through the gaps
CO₂ travels as bicarbonate, which bypasses the membrane
The kidneys excrete the extra CO₂ as it builds up
e: Diffusion depends on solubility; CO₂ is about 20 times more soluble than O₂, so it crosses a thickened membrane easily.
O₂ transfer suffers first. (CO₂ is actually the larger molecule, and the kidneys excrete H⁺ and HCO₃⁻, not CO₂ gas.)

q: During normal inhalation, the diaphragm:
e: Contraction enlarges the chest cavity, lowering pressure so air flows in.

q: Why is oxygen delivery to tissues in severe anemia low even when P(O₂) in arterial blood is normal?
o: There's less hemoglobin to carry O₂
The lungs can't take in O₂
e: Most O₂ in blood is carried by hemoglobin.
With little hemoglobin, total O₂ content drops even if saturation and P(O₂) are normal.

q: Why does gas exchange occur so efficiently across the alveolar wall?
o: Its thin wall and huge surface area allow rapid diffusion
Active transport pumps move O₂ into the capillary blood
Its thick wall stores O₂ for steady release into blood
Air pressure forces O₂ into the blood by bulk flow
e: Fick's law: diffusion rises with surface area and falls with wall thickness.

q: In pneumonia, some alveoli fill with fluid but still receive blood flow. Why does breathing 100% O₂ raise arterial P(O₂) only a little?
o: Blood through those alveoli never meets the added O₂
Fluid in the alveoli absorbs most of the extra O₂
Hemoglobin cannot bind O₂ in pneumonia patients
Extra O₂ slows breathing, so ventilation drops
e: Fluid-filled alveoli are perfused but not ventilated (a shunt), so their blood stays deoxygenated.
Blood from healthy alveoli is already nearly 100% saturated and can't carry much more, so mixing still gives low arterial P(O₂).

q: The kidney helps control blood pH mainly by:
o: Converting CO₂ into urea for excretion
Releasing hemoglobin to buffer the blood
e: This renal compensation is slower than breathing changes but very powerful.

q: A climber stays at high altitude for several days and breathes faster than normal, lowering blood CO₂. How do the kidneys compensate?
o: They excrete more HCO₃⁻ to bring blood pH back down
They reabsorb more HCO₃⁻ to raise blood pH further
They secrete more H⁺ into the urine to raise pH
They stop filtering blood until the pH returns to normal
e: Losing CO₂ removes acid, causing respiratory alkalosis (pH too high).
The kidneys reabsorb less HCO₃⁻ (and secrete less H⁺), so the extra base leaves in the urine. This takes days.

q: If blood glucose is very high, glucose appears in the urine. Why?
o: The loop of Henle secretes glucose
e: Reabsorption has a maximum (transport maximum).
Above about 180–200 mg dL⁻¹, extra glucose spills into urine.

q: A person's GFR is 120 mL min⁻¹ and plasma glucose is 1 mg mL⁻¹ (100 mg dL⁻¹). How much glucose is filtered into the nephrons each minute?
e: Filtered load = GFR × plasma concentration.
= 120 mL min⁻¹ × 1 mg mL⁻¹ = 120 mg min⁻¹

q: When blood pressure drops, angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole more than the afferent arteriole. How does this help the kidney?
o: It keeps glomerular pressure up so GFR is maintained
It lowers glomerular pressure so less fluid is filtered
It increases blood flow into the vasa recta
It stops filtration completely to save water
e: Narrowing the outflow vessel (efferent) backs blood up in the glomerulus.
Higher glomerular hydrostatic pressure helps keep GFR near normal even though less blood is arriving.
t: Squeeze the exit (efferent) and pressure rises upstream; squeeze the entrance (afferent) and it falls.

q: Constricting the afferent arteriole would cause GFR to:
e: Less blood enters the glomerulus, lowering glomerular pressure and filtration.
Constricting the efferent arteriole would raise GFR.

q: Urine leaves each kidney and travels to the bladder through the:
e: Each kidney has one ureter that carries urine down to the bladder.
The urethra carries urine from the bladder out of the body.
t: Ureters: two (one per kidney). Urethra: one (out of the body).

q: A patient's blood pH is 7.30 and their HCO₃⁻ is low. Their breathing is fast and deep. What is happening?
e: Low pH + low bicarbonate = metabolic acidosis.
Fast breathing blows off CO₂ to raise pH toward normal.

q: In very cold weather, the body reduces blood flow to the skin. What is the purpose?
o: To keep warm blood in the core and reduce heat loss
To raise skin temperature and prevent frostbite
To send more warm blood to the skin surface
To lower metabolism and conserve stored energy
e: Vasoconstriction in the skin conserves heat; shivering generates more.

q: Why does drinking alcohol increase urination?
e: Less ADH → fewer aquaporins in the collecting duct → more dilute urine.

q: A patient makes large volumes of dilute urine because his hypothalamus makes no ADH (central diabetes insipidus). What happens when he is given synthetic ADH (desmopressin)?
o: Urine volume falls and the urine becomes more concentrated
Nothing changes, because his collecting ducts lack ADH receptors
The urine becomes even more dilute
Glucose begins to appear in the urine
e: His collecting ducts and ADH receptors are normal; only the hormone is missing.
Supplying ADH inserts aquaporins, so water is reabsorbed into the salty medulla and less, more concentrated urine is made. A patient with nephrogenic DI would not respond.

q: The descending limb of the loop of Henle is permeable to ___, while the thick ascending limb actively pumps out ___.
e: Descending: water leaves into the salty medulla.
Ascending: impermeable to water but pumps out salt.

q: Which vessels contribute most to resistance and control blood flow to organs?
e: Arterioles have smooth muscle that constricts or dilates, adjusting resistance.

q: Mean arterial pressure is 100 mmHg and cardiac output is 5 L min⁻¹. What is total peripheral resistance?
e: MAP = CO × TPR, so TPR = MAP ÷ CO
100 ÷ 5 = 20 mmHg·min L⁻¹

q: Which blood cells carry oxygen?
e: Red blood cells are packed with hemoglobin and lack a nucleus and mitochondria.

q: A patient with liver failure makes too little albumin and develops swelling (edema). Why?
o: Lower plasma oncotic pressure means less fluid returns to capillaries
Higher plasma oncotic pressure pulls fluid out of the capillaries into tissue
Higher arterial blood pressure forces fluid out of all vessels
Capillaries become impermeable, trapping fluid in the tissues
e: Albumin creates most of the plasma's oncotic pressure.
With less albumin, fluid stays in the tissues.

q: Why does the AV node delay the electrical signal briefly?
o: So the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract
So the SA node can recharge before firing the next impulse
So the ventricles contract before the atria to prevent backflow
So the ventricles can repolarize, producing the T wave
e: The delay coordinates the timing of atrial and ventricular contraction.

q: A patient's ECG shows normal P waves, but some are not followed by QRS complexes. Where is the problem most likely located?
e: The atria are firing normally (P waves present).
The signal isn't always passing to the ventricles, pointing to the AV node.

q: What is the heart's natural pacemaker?
e: The SA node fires spontaneously and sets the heart rate.

q: On an ECG, the QRS complex represents:
e: P wave: atrial depolarization. QRS: ventricular depolarization. T wave: ventricular repolarization.

q: Why must the average output of the right ventricle equal that of the left ventricle?
o: The circuits are in series, so a mismatch would pool blood
Both ventricles share one pacemaker, so their volumes match
Both ventricles have walls of the same thickness and force
A hole in the septum lets their volumes equalize each beat
e: Blood from the right ventricle must pass through the lungs to reach the left side, then around the body back to the right.
If one side pumped even slightly more, blood would quickly build up in the other circuit (as in heart failure).

q: Which force mainly pushes fluid OUT of capillaries at the arterial end?
e: At the arterial end, hydrostatic pressure exceeds oncotic pressure, so fluid leaves.
At the venous end, oncotic pressure pulls fluid back in.

q: A blood clot blocks a deep vein in a patient's calf, and the lower leg swells. What is the main cause of the swelling?
o: Capillary hydrostatic pressure rises, so more fluid filters out
Plasma oncotic pressure rises, pulling fluid into the tissue
Lymph vessels begin pumping fluid into the tissue
Capillary walls become impermeable to water
e: Blood backs up behind the blocked vein, raising pressure in the upstream capillaries.
Higher capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes more fluid out than oncotic pressure can pull back, and once the lymphatics are overwhelmed, edema forms.
t: Edema = too much push (hydrostatic) or too little pull (oncotic, e.g. low albumin).

q: At extremely high heart rates (over about 180 beats per minute), cardiac output can actually fall. Why?
o: Diastole gets too short for the ventricles to fill
Systole becomes too short for the valves to open
The SA node runs out of its stored Ca²⁺
The atria and ventricles start contracting together
e: Faster rates shorten diastole much more than systole.
With too little filling time, end-diastolic volume and stroke volume drop enough that CO = HR × SV falls.

q: Bacteria in the large intestine are important because they:
o: Make vitamin K and some B vitamins
e: Gut bacteria ferment fiber and produce vitamins and short-chain fatty acids.

q: Fructose crosses the apical membrane of intestinal cells on a carrier protein (GLUT5), moving down its concentration gradient without Na⁺ or ATP. This type of transport is:
e: Fructose moves down its concentration gradient through the GLUT5 carrier, with no Na⁺ and no ATP needed.
That is facilitated diffusion: carrier-mediated but passive.

q: Where are disaccharide-digesting enzymes such as lactase and sucrase found?
o: On the brush border of small-intestine cells
In pancreatic juice released into the duodenum
In saliva released into the mouth
In gastric juice released by chief cells
e: Lactase, sucrase and maltase are built into the microvilli (brush border) membrane of enterocytes.
They split disaccharides into monosaccharides right where those sugars are absorbed.

q: Between meals, bile is stored and concentrated in the:
e: The liver makes bile continuously, but between meals it is sent to the gallbladder.
The gallbladder removes water to concentrate bile and releases it after a meal.

q: Why doesn't pepsin digest the stomach's own lining?
o: It's secreted as inactive pepsinogen, and mucus protects the lining
The lining is made mostly of lipids, which pepsin can't digest
Pepsin is active only at neutral pH, so stomach acid keeps it inactive
Parietal cells secrete a pepsin inhibitor into the lumen
e: Pepsinogen is activated by acid in the stomach's lumen.
Bicarbonate-rich mucus protects the epithelial cells.

q: A gallstone blocks the common bile duct for several weeks, so no bile reaches the intestine. Besides pale stools, which problem is expected?
o: Poor absorption of vitamins A, D, E and K
Very high blood glucose after meals
e: Without bile salts, fats are not emulsified or packed into micelles, so most dietary fat passes into the stool.
Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are absorbed along with fat in micelles, so their absorption falls too.
t: Anything that blocks fat absorption also blocks A, D, E and K.

q: Which ring of muscle controls how quickly chyme passes from the stomach into the duodenum?
e: The pyloric sphincter sits at the stomach's outlet and lets chyme into the duodenum a little at a time.
The lower esophageal sphincter guards the stomach's entrance; the ileocecal valve joins the small and large intestines.

q: Salivary amylase keeps digesting starch inside a swallowed mass of food for a while. Why does it eventually stop working in the stomach?
o: Stomach acid lowers the pH and denatures it
Bile salts in the stomach coat the starch
Pepsinogen binds amylase and blocks it
Body temperature in the stomach is too high
e: Amylase works best near neutral pH (about 7).
As gastric HCl soaks into the food mass, the pH drops to about 2 and amylase denatures.

q: In a classic experiment, researchers cut all the nerves to a loop of a dog's small intestine, then dripped acid into that loop. The pancreas still released bicarbonate-rich fluid. Injecting an extract of the intestinal lining into the blood had the same effect. What do these results show?
o: A chemical carried in the blood signals the pancreas
Nerves are required for the pancreas to respond
The acid itself travels to the pancreas and triggers it
The pancreas senses the stomach's pH directly
e: With the nerves to the intestine cut, the signal can't be neural.
An intestinal extract given into the blood mimicked the effect, so the intestine releases a blood-borne messenger: a hormone (secretin).
t: This was the discovery of the first hormone, secretin, in 1902.

q: Which structural features give the small intestine its huge absorptive surface?
e: Each level of folding multiplies the surface area.

q: Which enzyme digests most of the triglycerides (fats) in a meal?
e: Pancreatic lipase, released into the duodenum, splits triglycerides into fatty acids and monoglycerides.
Pepsin and trypsin digest proteins; pancreatic amylase digests starch.

q: A drug works poorly when swallowed because it is heavily broken down before it reaches the general circulation, but it works well when dissolved under the tongue. Why?
o: Gut-absorbed drugs pass through the liver first; sublingual ones skip it
Saliva activates the drug, but stomach acid does not
The tongue absorbs drugs faster than the stomach destroys them
Under-the-tongue drugs enter the lymph and then the liver
e: Drugs absorbed from the intestine travel through the hepatic portal vein to the liver, which can metabolize much of the dose (first-pass effect).
Veins under the tongue drain into the systemic circulation, bypassing the liver on the first pass.
t: 'First-pass metabolism' is why nitroglycerin is given under the tongue.

q: IgA is found mainly in:
o: Mucus, saliva, tears and breast milk
e: IgA protects mucosal surfaces.

q: In clonal selection, what happens when a B cell meets the antigen its receptor matches?
o: That B cell multiplies into many plasma cells and memory cells
All B cells multiply equally, regardless of their receptor
That B cell undergoes apoptosis to prevent autoimmunity
That B cell matures into a helper T cell that secretes cytokines
e: Only the matching clone is selected and expanded.

q: A typical antibody (IgG) molecule is made of:
o: Two heavy chains and two light chains
One heavy chain and one light chain
Two light chains and no heavy chains
e: IgG is a Y-shaped protein of two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains joined by disulfide bonds.
Each arm's tip, formed by both chains' variable regions, binds antigen.

q: An injection of antivenom after a snakebite provides:
e: Ready-made antibodies are given (passive) through medicine (artificial). Protection is immediate but short-lived.

q: During anaphylaxis, mast cells release histamine, causing widespread vasodilation and airway narrowing. Why is epinephrine the first-line treatment?
o: It constricts blood vessels and opens the airways
It destroys the IgE bound to the mast cells
It blocks antigen from reaching the mast cells
It kills the mast cells releasing histamine
e: Epinephrine acts on α₁ receptors to constrict vessels and raise blood pressure.
It acts on β₂ receptors to relax bronchial smooth muscle, directly reversing histamine's effects.

q: Natural killer cells attack cells that:
e: Some viruses and tumors hide by reducing MHC I.
NK cells detect this 'missing self' and kill the cell.

q: Weeks after immunization, a person's antibodies bind the antigen more tightly than early antibodies did. What explains this?
o: B cells with mutations that bind better are selected
Antibodies change shape over time in the blood
T cells start making higher-affinity antibodies
The antigen mutates to fit the antibodies better
e: In lymph node germinal centers, B cell antibody genes mutate rapidly (somatic hypermutation).
B cells whose receptors bind antigen best get survival signals and multiply: affinity maturation.

q: A person receives a tetanus vaccine. This is:
e: The body makes its own antibodies and memory (active) after a medical procedure (artificial).

q: In type 1 diabetes, immune cells destroy pancreatic β cells. What kind of disorder is this?
e: The immune system attacks the body's own cells, failing self-tolerance.

q: Which cells capture antigen in the tissues, travel to lymph nodes, and are the most effective at activating naive T cells?
e: Dendritic cells engulf antigen, migrate through lymph to nodes, and present peptides on MHC with costimulatory signals.
They bridge innate and adaptive immunity.

q: Which immune cells differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells?
e: Activated B cells can differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antibodies.

q: During an infection, pyrogens such as IL-1 cause fever by:
o: Raising the temperature set point in the hypothalamus
Directly heating the blood through bacterial metabolism
Blocking sweat glands so heat cannot leave the body
Speeding up the thyroid gland's release of T₄
e: Pyrogens trigger prostaglandin E₂ production in the hypothalamus, which raises the set point.
The body then conserves and makes heat (shivering, vasoconstriction) until it reaches the new set point.

q: Osteoclast activity increases when blood calcium is low. Which hormone drives this?
e: PTH indirectly activates osteoclasts to release calcium from bone.

q: Which layer of the skin contains blood vessels, sweat glands and hair follicles?
e: The dermis is the connective-tissue layer under the epidermis, with vessels, nerves, glands and follicles.
The epidermis (including the stratum corneum and stratum basale) has no blood vessels.

q: Bones are connected to muscles by:
e: Tendons: muscle to bone. Ligaments: bone to bone.

q: A motor unit consists of:
o: One motor neuron and all the muscle fibers it controls
One muscle fiber and all the neurons that reach it
One sarcomere and the Ca²⁺ stored around it
One muscle and the tendon attaching it to bone
e: Each motor neuron branches to contact many muscle fibers.
When the neuron fires, all of its fibers contract together.

q: A sprained ankle is a stretch or tear of the dense connective tissue that holds the bones of the joint together. This tissue is:
e: Ligaments connect bone to bone at joints.
Tendons attach muscle to bone; articular cartilage covers bone ends inside the joint.

q: People with darker skin living at high latitudes are at higher risk of vitamin D deficiency in winter. Which explanation fits best?
o: More melanin absorbs the UVB needed to make vitamin D
More melanin breaks down the vitamin D the skin makes
Darker skin has fewer cells containing cholesterol
Cold air blocks the skin from absorbing any light
e: Skin makes vitamin D when UVB converts 7-dehydrocholesterol.
Melanin absorbs UVB; where winter sunlight is weak, less UVB reaches that precursor, so less vitamin D is made.

q: Why do long bones in children grow in length but adult bones do not?
o: Children's growth plates are still active cartilage; adults' have fused
Adults have no osteoblasts, so new bone matrix can't be laid down
Children's bones lack calcium, so they lengthen under mechanical load
Adults completely stop secreting growth hormone after puberty
e: Cartilage at the growth plates divides and is replaced by bone.
After puberty, the plates close (ossify).

q: A child with severe vitamin D deficiency develops soft, bowed leg bones. What is the main cause?
o: Too little Ca²⁺ is absorbed to mineralize new bone
Osteoblasts stop producing any new bone matrix
Too much Ca²⁺ is deposited in the growing bones
Growth plates fuse too early and stop all bone growth
e: Active vitamin D (calcitriol) is needed to absorb Ca²⁺ and phosphate from the gut.
Without enough mineral, newly made matrix stays soft and bends under weight (rickets).

q: Which type of muscle fiber resists fatigue and relies on aerobic metabolism?
e: Type I fibers have many mitochondria and myoglobin, giving them a red color and endurance.

q: Torn knee cartilage heals much more slowly than a broken bone. Why?
o: Cartilage is made mostly of calcium phosphate
Cartilage is constantly broken down by osteoclasts
e: Cartilage is avascular, so nutrients and repair cells reach it only slowly by diffusion.
Bone has a rich blood supply that brings cells and nutrients for repair.

q: Osteons (Haversian systems), with rings of matrix around a central canal, are the structural units of:
e: Compact bone is built from tightly packed osteons; each central canal carries blood vessels and nerves.
Spongy bone is a lattice of thin struts (trabeculae) without osteons.

q: Which bone cells build new bone matrix?
e: Osteoblasts build bone; osteoclasts break it down; osteocytes maintain it.
t: osteoBlasts Build; osteoClasts Chew.

q: Which labeled segment is impermeable to water but actively pumps out Na⁺ and Cl⁻, building the salty medulla?
e: D is the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle.
C (descending limb) is permeable to water.

e: 1 marks the dendrites, which receive input.
